segments: The seventeenth dynasty.
The Arab kings.
And the males indeed they killed,
and the females they sent to Qaraqorum.
Then he was consumed with great distress,
and became afflicted with a severe sickness,
and departed from the world on that island,
and they buried him there.
And after a time,
he was transferred {OCR?} to the fortress called Ardahin (Ardahan?).
When Jalal al-Din, the son of Sultan Muhammad, heard of his father's death,
in a single night he went forty parasangs towards the lands of the Persians,
those that are on the border of India.
And there gathered to him ninety thousand chosen cavalry.
Genghis
Khan, when he heard that Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah was again growing strong, even more than his father,
sent against him a large force of Mongols.
And Jalal al-Din heard [of it],
and went out to meet them.
And when he encountered the Tatars,
he said to the men of his party,
and they all dismounted,
and each one held his horse by its hand [reins].
And they despised death,
and cast many of the Mongols to the ground with arrows until the evening.
And that night each of the two sides passed the night in its place.
And on the second day,
when the Tatars saw the courage of the Khwarazmians,
they turned their faces to flee.
And the Khwarazmians pursued after them,
and killed about five hundred champions of the Tatars.
Now when Genghis Khan heard these things,
he arrived like lightning with a large force that surpassed counting.
And as soon as Jalal al-Din saw them,
he knew that their force could not be resisted.
And on this account, he set his face to cross the Gihon river to the east,
and sent to prepare boats.
Now Genghis Khan heard these things,
and sent a large army before him and seized his route.
And then no other hope remained to him,
except to fight until the last breath.
And the battle was joined between the two sides,
and the right wing {OCR?} of the Khwarazmians was broken,
and again their left wing was broken.
And Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah himself remained in the center with only seven hundred horsemen,
and like a wolf he was leaping from side to side,
and striking down slain men from among the Tatars.
And the Mongols were increasing more and more, and descending upon him from all sides.
Then a certain Khwarazmian emir,
who was the maternal cousin of Jalal al-Din himself,
seized the reins of his horse,
